<meta>This page continues the investigation into the precise geographical boundaries of the land promised to Abraham, specifically addressing the southwestern border at the "River of Egypt" and comparing biblical descriptions with historical and linguistic evidence.</meta>

# HISTORY OF THE HEBREW CHURCH. Chapter V.

<margin>
* See also our marginal commentators on Joshua 13:3.
</margin>

<margin>
The Nile and Sichor both named for their black color.
</margin>

<margin>
And how this river on the side of Egypt or the Southwest forms the boundaries of Canaan. And why it is slightly changed in our small map. *
</margin>

...to determine the boundaries; but also even from the name of the river *Sichor*: for just as *Sichor* <note>original Hebrew: שִׁיחוֹר (Shihor), meaning black or dark</note> means "blackish," it is generally testified that the Nile stream has blackish water; so that it is the same as if one said, *The Black River*: just as here with us, it is still called the *Swarte Water* <note>The Zwarte Water (Black Water) is a river in the Netherlands; the author uses this local comparison to help his Dutch readers understand the naming convention.</note>. Likewise the Greeks, according to Plutarchus and Eustathius, also called this river *Melas* <note>Greek: Μέλας, meaning black.</note>, and the Latins *Melo*, after its black color. Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a renowned Dutch scholar of history and chronology.</note> also derived the word *Sirin*, with which the Ethiopians name the Nile, from the Hebrew word *Sichor*; as has been noted elsewhere in the *Jewish Antiquities*. In such a way that one must at least likely conclude that *Nahal* <note>Hebrew for "brook" or "valley river."</note> and *Sichor* here do not mean the Nile any further than that we should understand by them merely an arm of that great river which flows out at Rhinokorrura <note>A coastal town between Egypt and Palestine, modern-day El Arish.</note>. Thus all the maps in the magnificent atlases and the Bible maps are deficient in this regard and need to be corrected. For although most are not negligent in making this river a boundary of Judea, they nevertheless show it so wide and emerging entirely on its own that no one could ever have considered it an arm of the Nile. Perhaps Strabo <note>A Greek geographer from the 1st century BCE/CE.</note> indicated it better, who, above the great Pelusian mouth of the Nile, places a smaller river by Mount Casius; to which he, along with many other writers, extends the boundary of Judea. Being, however, not so very far from Rhinokorrura, which city was so named after the truncated noses of its citizens <note>The name Rhinokorrura comes from the Greek for "cut-off noses," referring to a legend that the city was a penal colony for criminals whose noses had been mutilated.</note>. Therefore, it should seem strange to no one that a small change is perceived in our map in this vicinity. And although this river is so small that it only deserves the name of a *brook* and was not even navigable by any vessels, it should not surprise us when Holy Scripture calls it the *River of Egypt* and *Sichor*, as if it intended to signify the great bosom of the Nile itself thereby; since it is very common that in things of the same kind, especially water, the name of the whole is also given to its part. As for what further concerns the Nile stream itself, we shall speak more extensively of that in another place.

<margin>
Boundaries of Canaan indicated to the North and Northeast.
</margin>

<margin>
Whether Abraham's descendants ever possessed the Land of Canaan in the extent promised, namely from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates or the Great River.
</margin>

If we have then correctly found the divine boundary of Canaan to the South or Southwest against Egypt, we have no more difficulty remaining in discovering the same to the North or Northeast at the Euphrates, which Moses, not unjustly, calls *The Great River*. As to which our map sufficiently indicates the situation of its course; already described enough by us previously. But there another dispute arises to be brought from black darkness into the light: namely, how and where one shall correctly place the fulfillment of the promise in this wide region of the land? Since not only did the Jews never have all the provinces situated between these two rivers—the Nile and the Euphrates—in hereditary possession (which is nevertheless promised in plain words); but also, in Numbers 34, the possession of the land is not given to Israel further than *Hamath*, which is truly still very far on this side of the Euphrates. But let us hear the opinions of the scholars and then choose which one we wish to support. Jerome <note>original: Hieronymus, the 4th-century Church Father who translated the Vulgate.</note>, and after him Masius <note>Andreas Masius (1514–1573), a Flemish priest and humanist scholar of the Near East.</note> with others, are of the opinion that the promise of such a broad possession of the land was made under the condition of a laudable obedience on the part of Abraham's seed, that is *Israel*: which not having been proven by them later, God was released from His word of promise and was not bound to fulfill it to the end. To which one might remark that if the promise was made under condition, such an implicit condition must then rather apply to the whole promise and not only to certain parts of it...

From this I infer: that for the <term>introit</term> <note>the opening chant of the Mass</note>, the <term>responsory</term>, and the <term>short responsory</term> <note>a brief chant used in the Divine Office</note>—because they contain verses with a faster pace or repetition (though the verse must be examined for how much it rises or falls as part of the mode)—you should not look at the final note of the verse, but rather where you stop singing, which is the last note before the verse begins. Count five notes up from the final note; if the melody rises further above those five than it descends below its final note, it will be a <term>master</term> <note>original: "maestro"; refers to an authentic mode</note>. And if it descends below its final note more than it rises above the aforementioned five notes, it will be a <term>disciple</term> <note>original: "discipulo"; refers to a plagal mode</note>. If they are equal (rising as many notes above the five as it descends below the final), it shall be a <term>master</term>, a status granted as an honor—unless the clef or a particular passage indicates it belongs to the disciples, in which case it will not be a master. You will find this rule explained in the following four examples.

Although this knowledge is imperfect and general, it is easy to learn. For every chant that ends in <term>E-la-mi</term> <note>the note E</note> or in <term>F-fa-ut</term> <note>the note F</note>, look at the clef it carries, and you will understand by this alone which mode it is. If it is the <term>F-fa-ut</term> clef <note>F-clef</note>, such a mode will be a <term>disciple</term>; and if it is the <term>C-sol-fa-ut</term> clef <note>C-clef</note>, we shall say that mode is a <term>master</term>. Every <term>tract</term> <note>a solo chant used in the Mass during penitential seasons</note> in the Roman rite belongs to either the second or eighth mode. If such a chant ends in <term>D-sol-re</term> <note>the note D</note>, it will be of the second tone; and if it ends in <term>G-sol-re-ut</term> <note>the note G</note>, it will be the eighth mode. Every <term>short responsory</term>, whether it has an "Alleluia" or is sung without it, belongs to the sixth mode—except for *Into your hands, O Lord* <note>original: "In manus tuas domine"</note> without the "Alleluia" sung at Compline, those for the Lord's Advent at all the Hours, and the responsory for Terce on Sundays throughout the year (which begins *Incline my heart, O God* <note>original: "Inclina cor meu̅ deus"</note>), all of which belong to the fourth mode.

<column-break/>

We call <term>short responsories</term> those sung during the Hours after the Little Chapter <note>a short scripture reading</note>. What I say regarding short responsories pertains to the Roman rite. Concerning the recognition of <term>antiphons</term> <note>short chants sung before and after a psalm</note>, common and useful rules are set down in the arts of singing; specifically: first mode is *re-la*, second is *re-fa*, third is *mi-fa*, fourth is *mi-la*, fifth is *fa-fa*, sixth is *fa-la*, seventh is *ut-sol*, and eighth is *ut-fa*. But for greater brevity and certainty, I say: If the <term>sequence</term> <note>original: "sequencia"; here referring to the "differentia" or the melodic ending of the psalm tone</note> or the *World without end, Amen* <note>original: "seculoru̅ amen"; the concluding phrase of the Gloria Patri</note> begins three or four notes above the final note, it will be a <term>disciple</term>; and if it is five or six notes, it will be a <term>master</term>. The <term>sequence</term> of a master mode always begins, by right of its preeminence, higher than that of a disciple. One can also recognize these antiphons at the beginning by the interval from the final note up to the note where the sequence begins. If at the start it says *re-la* step-by-step or by a leap, it will be the first mode; if *re-fa*, it will be the second; and so on for all other modes according to the rule above. In this way, the rule that serves for the end of the antiphon and the beginning of the sequence also applies to the beginning of the said antiphon. If you ever find otherwise, understand it to be an error of the scribe or a fault of the composer, because the rule is infallible.

The perfect knowledge of the other modes is as follows. By rule, a mode has the capacity to rise five notes above its final, which is a <term>diapente</term> <note>the interval of a fifth</note>. To be a <term>master</term>, it will add four notes—a <term>diatessaron</term> <note>the interval of a fourth</note>—above that fifth. To be a <term>disciple</term>, it will carry the <term>diatessaron</term> below its final note. Any mode lacking any of the eight points mentioned above shall be called <term>imperfect</term>. Thus, for a mode to be perfect, it must have eight points, which constitute a <term>diapason</term> <note>the interval of an octave</note>. I say that five points and four points make eight because the one note that is the end of the <term>diapente</term> is counted twice, as it is also the beginning of the <term>diatessaron</term>. All modes, both masters and disciples, have two notes of "license" <note>allowable notes outside the strict modal range</note> to make the final cadences of the <term>diapason</term>. We might wonder about this, because it is commonly said among musicians that all modes carry these two notes of license. Why are these two notes called "license" rather than part of the eight notes all modes carry? Or if the eight are by rule, why are the two not also by rule? There is a difference between being "by art" <note>governed by formal rules</note> and being "by license." The Latins took the art of music from the Greeks, who gave the modes only one <term>diapason</term>, which is eight notes.

It defines the mathematical structure of the octave as a combination of a fifth and a fourth and explains the concept of musical 'license' regarding range.</summary>

7. "Found"—22. "Found": by placing the same word at the beginning and the end of the story, the poet wittily marks the beginning and end of the myth; cf. Olympian I 93, Pythian X 51 — 10. "Flowing": cf. "they poured forth a wail" in Isthmian VIII 58 — 11ff. Pindar follows Hesiod's *Theogony* 274ff., except that here he makes Minerva a patron of Perseus, as also in Pythian X 45; in this, he is followed by Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V 250, "Tritonia gave herself as a companion to her gold-born brother," and Apollodorus II 41 — 13. "Darkened": he blinded them by taking away the one communal eye which the daughters of Phorcys, that is, the Gorgons (so the scholia and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV 773; Apollodorus II 37 distinguishes between the Phorcides and the Gorgons), used alternately — 14. Perseus, son of Danae, turned the love of Polydectes, king of the island of Seriphos, for his mother Danae and the symbol he had demanded for his marriage to Hippodamia, into destruction; for, having brought the head of Medusa as a symbol, he turned the island and Polydectes into stone; cf. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V 242ff. — 16. "Beautiful cheeks": in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV 792, she is of the most brilliant beauty. From this, artists started wanting to portray the head of Medusa as an image of the highest beauty not extinguished even by death, and later poets imagined that Medusa had competed with Minerva for beauty — 17. "Son of Danae": placed with emphasis at the beginning of a new strophe, as in Olympian II 105, III 6, X 34, Pythian I 7, IV 185, XI 22, Isthmian VI 35, III 73 — 19. "Maiden": he placed this in the middle so it would be the subject of two verbs, "rescued" and "fashioned" — "All-sounding melody": cf. Olympian VII 12 — 20. "Euryale": the name of one of the Gorgons; he omitted the name of the third sister, Stheno — 22. "To mortal men to have": whether this alludes to the well-known myth about the goddess throwing away the flutes because they deformed her face is uncertain.

<header>THE PEACE, 1174-1192</header>

It is, he says, true Sardian tincture, <note>A high-quality, expensive red dye.</note>
Which they guarantee will not run;
But if ever it gets to fighting,
Though his scarlet coat be on,
He himself becomes as pallid
As the palest Cyzicene, <note>A reference to coins or people from the city of Cyzicus.</note>
Running like a tawny cockhorse,
He is the first to quit the scene;
His crests shake and quake above him:
I stood gaping while he fled.
Ah, but when at home they are stationed,
Things that cannot be borne they do,
Making up the lists unfairly,
Striking out and putting down
Names at random. It is tomorrow
That the soldiers leave the town;
One poor wretch has bought no victuals,
For he knew not he must go
Till he on Pandion’s <note>A statue in the Athenian marketplace where official notices were posted.</note> statue
Spied the list and found it was so,
Reading there his name inserted;
Off he scuds with a wry face.
This is how they treat the farmers,
But the burghers certainly
Somewhat better: godless wretches,
Rogues with neither shame nor—shield,
Who one day, if God be willing,
Strict accounts to me shall yield.
For they have wronged me much and sorely:
Very lions in the city,
Very foxes in the fight.
Hillo! Hillo!
What lots are coming to the wedding supper!

<summary>The speaker denounces the hypocrisy of officials who act brave in the city but are cowards in battle, and who manipulate military conscription lists to the detriment of the farmers.</summary>
